title: Device-Independent Conference Keys from Parity-Extended Games
authors: Suvradip Chakraborty, Ronak Ramachandran, Aniruddha Sen
abstract: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) lets a group of parties establish a shared secret key from untrusted quantum devices, with security certified by non-locality. Existing DI-CKA protocols are each built around a single Bell inequality, typically a multiparty variant of the CHSH game. DI-QKD protocols, in contrast, have been built from a much richer landscape of non-local games, and it has remained unclear how to carry this landscape over to the conference setting. We introduce $\textit{Parity-$G$ games}$, which extend any two-player game $G$ to $N$ players, for every $N$, provided $G$ has an optimal strategy in which one player measures Pauli observables. The extension preserves the quantum and classical values of $G$, and the security of the resulting $N$-party protocol follows from an analysis of the two-player game alone. Our framework recovers the Parity-CHSH game of Ribeiro, Murta and Wehner (Phys. Rev. A, 2018) as a special case. Applied to the Mermin--Peres Magic Square Game, it yields a new $N$-player pseudo-telepathy game, the $\textit{Parity Magic Square Game}$, which ideal devices win in every round. We use it to construct the $\textit{first}$ DI-CKA protocol based on a pseudo-telepathy game. We prove the protocol secure against coherent attacks. It produces up to two key bits per round, and at low noise its key rate exceeds that of the DI-CKA protocol based on the Parity-CHSH game.
summary: This paper introduces Parity-G games, a novel framework to generalize two-player non-local games to $N$ parties for Device-Independent Conference Key Agreement (DI-CKA). By applying this to the Magic Square Game, the authors construct a new DI-CKA protocol that is provably secure and demonstrates a superior key rate compared to existing protocols in the low-noise regime.
main_problem: Developing scalable and secure Device-Independent Conference Key Agreement (DI-CKA) protocols for $N$ parties, overcoming the limitation of relying on single, multi-party Bell inequalities.
main_result: The authors introduce Parity-G games, constructing the first DI-CKA protocol based on a pseudo-telepathy game (pMSGN) that achieves a key rate exceeding protocols based on Parity-CHSH in the low noise regime.
method: The core method is the Parity-G framework, which generalizes any two-player Pauli game $G$ to $N$ players, allowing security analysis to reduce to the two-party game $G$.
model_or_system: The protocol utilizes untrusted multipartite quantum states shared among $N$ parties, testing non-locality via generalized Pauli games like the Mermin–Peres Magic Square Game (pMSGN).
key_observables: Key rate ($r_\infty$), winning probability ($\omega$), and conditional von Neumann entropy $H(A|E)$.
important_parameters: Noise probability ($q$), number of parties ($N$), and the threshold for non-zero key bits ($\omega_{tol} > 8/9$).
main_assumptions: The security proof relies on reducing the $N$-party security to the underlying two-party game $G$, and the analysis assumes the existence of an untrusted multipartite state $ho$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Alice's Pauli measurements for the MSG game and the referee's correction bits for the $pMSGN$ protocol.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the Parity-G framework, applies it to the Mermin–Peres Magic Square Game to construct the pMSGN-based DI-CKA protocol, proves its security against coherent attacks, and compares its key rate to existing protocols.
why_interesting: The work provides a general, scalable framework for constructing multi-party quantum cryptographic protocols whose security is certified by non-locality, which is fundamental to quantum information theory.
